#### 7.4 Step by step

##### Step 1: collect the usable indexes

`get_relation_info()` opens every index of the table. It skips an index whose `indisvalid` is false; the executor may still insert into it, but the planner never reads it ([plancat.c:256-267](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L256-L267)). It also skips an index whose `indcheckxmin` horizon has not passed for this transaction, and marks the plan transient so the plan cache rebuilds it later ([plancat.c:269-281](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L269-L281)).

E7.14 shows the invalid case. A `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on the duplicate-laden `status` column failed and left the index behind. Measured, E7.14:

```text
      index       | indisvalid | indisready
 orders_status_uq | f          | f
...
 Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..601.00 rows=1509 width=40)
   Filter: (status = 'cancelled'::text)
```

A valid index on the same column, built inside a rolled-back transaction, gave a `Bitmap Heap Scan` for the same query (E7.14). So the sequential scan above is not a cost decision: the broken index was never offered.

For each usable index, the planner records the column keys, operator families, collations and returnable columns ([plancat.c:283-310](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L283-L310)), the AM's capability flags ([plancat.c:318-331](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L318-L331)), the ordering information ([plancat.c:340-415](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L340-L415)), and any expressions and predicate ([plancat.c:447-452](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L447-L452)). A non-partial index takes the table's row estimate as its tuple count; a partial index is sized like a table and capped at the table's rows; a B-tree also records its height ([plancat.c:466-500](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L466-L500)). Finally `get_relation_info_hook` may add a [hypothetical index](../../../glossary.md#hypothetical-index) or remove entries ([plancat.c:575-576](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L575-L576)).

##### Step 2: prove partial-index predicates

During the size pass, `check_index_predicates()` gathers the table's restriction clauses, the join clauses that may be moved to it, and clauses implied by equivalence classes. It asks `predicate_implied_by()` whether they imply the index predicate, and stores the answer in `predOK` ([indxpath.c:3272-3316](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L3272-L3316), [indxpath.c:3348-3350](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L3348-L3350)). The proof uses "strong" implication: truth of the clauses must force truth of the predicate ([predtest.c:116-151](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/predtest.c#L116-L151)).

When the proof succeeds, the quals the predicate already guarantees are dropped from the index's `indrestrictinfo`, so the plan does not re-check them. This is skipped for an `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE` or `FOR UPDATE` target, because EvalPlanQual rechecks need the original quals ([indxpath.c:3317-3378](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L3317-L3378)). E7.10 shows the effect: the `status = 'pending'` qual vanished from the plan.

```text
 Index Scan using orders_pending_cust on orders  (cost=0.28..8.30 rows=1 width=40)
   Index Cond: (customer_id = 700)
```

The proof compares an operator against a constant. When the query's side is not a `Const`, as with `status = $1` in a generic plan, the B-tree proof gives up ([predtest.c:1842-1858](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/predtest.c#L1842-L1858)). E7.10's generic plan (forced with `plan_cache_mode`, a forced setting) therefore used the full index, while the custom plan used the partial one:

```text
 Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=4.40..53.03 rows=5 width=40)
   Recheck Cond: (customer_id = $2)
   Filter: (status = $1)
...
 Index Scan using orders_pending_cust on orders  (cost=0.28..8.30 rows=1 width=40)
   Index Cond: (customer_id = 700)
```

[Pros and Cons of Partial Indexes in PostgreSQL 17 (unverified)](../indexing/partial-indexes-pros-cons.md) covers predicate proofs in more depth.

##### Step 3: match each clause to an index column

`match_clause_to_index()` refuses pseudoconstant clauses and clauses that must wait for a lower security level ([indxpath.c:2090-2106](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2090-L2106)). For the rest, `match_clause_to_indexcol()` sorts by clause shape: boolean columns, operator clauses, function clauses, [`ScalarArrayOpExpr`](../../../glossary.md#scalararrayopexpr), row comparisons and `IS [NOT] NULL` ([indxpath.c:2211-2266](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2211-L2266)).

An operator clause matches exactly when four things hold ([indxpath.c:2425-2447](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2425-L2447)):

1. One side is the index key. For an expression index, the side must be `equal()` to the stored expression ([indxpath.c:3715-3742](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L3715-L3742)).
2. The other side has no Var of this table and nothing volatile. Vars of other tables are allowed; they make the path parameterized.
3. The collation matches: `IndexCollMatchesExprColl` requires the index collation to be absent or identical to the clause's ([indxpath.c:39-40](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L39-L40)).
4. The operator is in the column's operator family. If the key is on the right, the commutator must be in the family, and the planner builds a commuted clause ([indxpath.c:2462-2487](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2462-L2487)).

An operator family can contain cross-type operators. `btree/integer_ops` includes `=(int4,int8)` ([pg_amop.dat:101-113](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_amop.dat#L101-L113)), so E7.2's `id = 42::bigint` became `Index Cond: (id = '42'::bigint)`. In contrast, `id + 0 = 42` is not the key at all, so E7.2 fell back to a `Seq Scan` with rows estimated by the default equality selectivity.

The collation test is strict identity, not equivalent behavior. In E3.12 the column uses the database default collation, which is C here, and the query asks for `"C"` explicitly. The index is ignored:

```text
 Index Scan using customers_name_idx on customers  (cost=0.28..8.29 rows=1 width=56)
   Index Cond: (name = 'customer 0042'::text)
...
 Seq Scan on customers  (cost=0.00..47.00 rows=1 width=56)
   Filter: (name = 'customer 0042'::text COLLATE "C")
```

When the operator is not in the family, the planner asks the operator's underlying function for help. `get_index_clause_from_support()` sends a `SupportRequestIndexCondition` to the function's planner support function, which may return derived index conditions, lossy by default ([indxpath.c#get_index_clause_from_support](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2557-L2615), [supportnodes.h#SupportRequestIndexCondition](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/nodes/supportnodes.h#L223-L240)). `LIKE` with a fixed prefix is the classic case: `textlike_support` builds `>=` and `<` bounds from the prefix ([like_support.c:192-229](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/like_support.c#L192-L229)). The range bounds need a C-collated index or a `*_pattern_ops` opclass, because other collations do not sort by prefix ([like_support.c:428-437](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/like_support.c#L428-L437)). E7.12:

```text
 Index Scan using customers_name_idx on customers  (cost=0.28..11.53 rows=101 width=56)
   Index Cond: ((name >= 'customer 01'::text) AND (name < 'customer 02'::text))
   Filter: (name ~~ 'customer 01%'::text)
```

The `Filter` line is there because the derived clause is lossy. Plan creation drops a scan clause only when it is the index clause itself, derived from the same equivalence class, or provably implied by the index conditions; a lossy clause matches none of these ([createplan.c:3050-3090](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/createplan.c#L3050-L3090)).

Range containment works differently. `elem_contained_by_range_support` answers a `SupportRequestSimplify` during constant folding, not an index request ([rangetypes.c#elem_contained_by_range_support](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/rangetypes.c#L2187-L2207)). When the range is a constant, it rewrites `x <@ range` into plain bound comparisons before any index matching runs ([rangetypes.c#find_simplified_clause-bounds](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/rangetypes.c#L2786-L2856)). Constant folding reaches it through the operator's function ([clauses.c:2632-2660](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c#L2632-L2660), [clauses.c:4113-4152](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c#L4113-L4152)). This support function was committed in the 17 development cycle (`075df6b208`). E7.12 shows no `Filter` left, because the rewrite is exact:

```text
 Index Scan using orders_ordered_at_idx on orders  (cost=0.29..9.99 rows=85 width=40)
   Index Cond: ((ordered_at >= '2024-06-01 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone) AND (ordered_at < '2024-06-02 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone))
```

The remaining clause shapes have their own gates. `= ANY (array)` needs a pseudo-constant array; `ALL` never matches ([indxpath.c:2638-2670](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2638-L2670)). Row comparisons such as `(a, b) > (1, 2)` match only B-tree indexes ([indxpath.c:2706-2708](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2706-L2708)). `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` match when the AM sets `amsearchnulls` ([indxpath.c:2251-2266](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2251-L2266)), which E7.4 shows as `Index Cond: (note IS NOT NULL)`.

##### Step 4: turn matches into index paths

`build_index_paths()` first gathers the matched clauses in column order. An AM without `amoptionalkey`, which among the built-ins is only hash, gets no path unless the first column has a clause ([indxpath.c:862-897](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L862-L897), [hash.c:69](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L69)). Every other AM may scan with a clause on a later column only, or with none, which means reading the whole index.

Next it works out ordering. An ordered index yields pathkeys in index order, kept only if a later step can use them; an AM with `amcanorderbyop` can instead return rows ordered by an operator such as `<->` ([indxpath.c:905-947](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L905-L947)). A backward scan is tried when the reversed order is useful ([indxpath.c:1005-1054](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1005-L1054)).

Then it checks for an index-only scan: every column the query needs from this table must be a returnable index column ([indxpath.c#check_index_only](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1730-L1800)). Expression columns are ignored in that check ([indxpath.c:1776-1785](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1776-L1785)). A [covering index](../../../glossary.md#covering-index) with `INCLUDE (amount)` passes it (E7.11).

A path is made when at least one of four reasons holds: it has clauses, a useful order, a proven predicate, or an index-only possibility ([indxpath.c:955-976](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L955-L976)). A parallel copy is tried when the AM sets `amcanparallel`, which only B-tree does ([indxpath.c:979-1002](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L979-L1002), [nbtree.c:119](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/nbtree/nbtree.c#L119)).

`get_index_paths()` then routes each path. It goes to `add_path` only if the AM can return tuples one by one (`amgettuple`), and it becomes a bitmap candidate only if the AM can build a bitmap and the path is selective ([indxpath.c:740-752](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L740-L752)). If the AM cannot evaluate `= ANY` natively, those clauses are left out of plain paths and tried again in bitmap-only paths ([indxpath.c:754-766](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L754-L766)).

##### Step 5: combine indexes through bitmaps

Every bitmap candidate for a table competes for one `BitmapHeapPath`. OR clauses whose every arm matches some index become a `BitmapOr` ([indxpath.c:312-326](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L312-L326), [indxpath.c#generate_bitmap_or_paths](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1180-L1255)). `choose_bitmap_and()` then sorts the candidates by cost and greedily adds each further index to a [BitmapAnd](../../../glossary.md#bitmapand) only while the estimated total keeps falling ([indxpath.c:1302-1328](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1302-L1328), [indxpath.c:1414-1489](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1414-L1489)).

E6.4 shows both outcomes. On the 226-page `orders` table, `customer_id = 7 AND ordered_at < '2024-03-01'` used one index and a filter, because ANDing could not save heap pages worth its cost. On the 6,819-page `events` table, two uncorrelated indexes were ANDed (E6.4c):

```text
         ->  BitmapAnd  (cost=731.08..731.08 rows=622 width=0) (actual rows=0 loops=1)
               ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_order_mod_idx  (cost=0.00..70.92 rows=6200 width=0) (actual rows=6200 loops=1)
               ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_kind_idx  (cost=0.00..659.59 rows=60156 width=0) (actual rows=60156 loops=1)
```

##### Step 6: parameterized index paths for joins

Join clauses and equivalence-class clauses that mention another table produce parameterized paths: the index condition takes its comparison value from the current outer row ([indxpath.c:283-310](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L283-L310)). The path cannot know yet how often it will run, so `get_loop_count()` assumes as many times as the smallest outer relation it depends on has rows ([indxpath.c#get_loop_count](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1829-L1872)). E7.13 ran such a path five times inside a nested loop:

```text
   ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders o  (cost=4.40..47.24 rows=15 width=10) (actual rows=10 loops=5)
         Recheck Cond: (c.id = customer_id)
```

[Chapter 8](#chapter-8-search-join-orders-and-methods) shows how join search uses these paths.

##### Step 7: cost each path

`cost_index()` calls the AM's `amcostestimate` for the index part, then prices the heap visits ([costsize.c:606-626](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L606-L626)). Each AM has its own estimator: `btcostestimate`, `hashcostestimate`, `gistcostestimate`, `spgcostestimate`, `gincostestimate` and `brincostestimate`, most of them built on `genericcostestimate` ([selfuncs.c#genericcostestimate-head](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/selfuncs.c#L6627-L6700), [selfuncs.c#hashcostestimate](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/selfuncs.c#L7214-L7254)). An index-only scan scales heap visits by `1 - allvisfrac`, both for a single scan and for a repeated one ([costsize.c:725-726](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L725-L726), [costsize.c:685-686](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L685-L686)). [Planner Penalties for Bloated Indexes in PostgreSQL 17 (unverified)](bloated-indexes-query-planner.md) walks through `btcostestimate` in depth.

A bitmap heap path starts with the bitmap's index cost and then charges each heap page between `random_page_cost` and `seq_page_cost`, interpolated by the square root of the fraction of pages read ([costsize.c:1044-1068](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L1044-L1068)). It assumes every row is rechecked, because a bitmap may become lossy ([costsize.c:1073-1085](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L1073-L1085)).

#### 7.5 Eligibility and comparison

The six built-in access methods differ in what they can offer, and those flags decide eligibility before any cost is computed. Measured, E7.1 (catalog properties):

```text
 amname | can_order | can_unique | can_multi_col | can_exclude | can_include
 brin   | f         | f          | t             | f           | f
 btree  | t         | t          | t             | t           | t
 gin    | f         | f          | t             | f           | f
 gist   | f         | f          | t             | t           | t
 hash   | f         | f          | f             | t           | f
 spgist | f         | f          | f             | t           | t
...
   index   | index_scan | bitmap_scan | backward_scan | orderable | distance_orderable | returnable | search_array | search_nulls
 am_btree  | t          | t           | t             | t         | f                  | t          | t            | t
 am_hash   | t          | t           | t             | f         | f                  | f          | f            | f
 am_gist   | t          | t           | f             | f         | t                  | t          | f            | t
 am_spgist | t          | t           | f             | f         | t                  | t          | f            | t
 am_gin    | f          | t           | f             | f         | f                  | f          | f            | f
 am_brin   | f          | t           | f             | f         | f                  | f          | f            | t
```

These properties are read from the AM routine: `index_scan` means `amgettuple` exists and `bitmap_scan` means `amgetbitmap` exists ([amutils.c:355-375](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/amutils.c#L355-L375)).

| Access method | Plain / index-only scan | Bitmap scan | Ordered output | Matched clauses | Source flags | Measured |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B-tree | Both; parallel too | Yes | Index order, both directions | `<`, `<=`, `=`, `>=`, `>` in the opfamily, `= ANY`, row comparisons, `IS [NOT] NULL` | [nbtree.c:108-144](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/nbtree/nbtree.c#L108-L144) | E7.2, E7.3, E7.4 |
| [Hash](../../../glossary.md#hash-index) | Plain only | Yes | None | `=` only; the first column must have a clause | [hash.c:64-100](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L64-L100), [pg_amop.dat:986-990](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_amop.dat#L986-L990) | E7.5: `email > 'user99'` falls back to a seq scan |
| [GiST](../../../glossary.md#gist) | Both | Yes | By distance operator (`<->`), forward only | Opclass strategies such as `<@`; `IS [NOT] NULL` | [gist.c:66-102](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gist.c#L66-L102), [pg_amop.dat:1134-1139](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_amop.dat#L1134-L1139) | E7.6 |
| [SP-GiST](../../../glossary.md#sp-gist) | Both | Yes | By distance operator | Opclass strategies; `IS [NOT] NULL` | [spgutils.c:51-87](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/spgist/spgutils.c#L51-L87), [pg_amop.dat:1502-1507](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_amop.dat#L1502-L1507) | E7.6 |
| [GIN](../../../glossary.md#gin) | Neither (`amgettuple` is NULL) | Only access path | None | Opclass strategies such as `@>` | [ginutil.c:44-80](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L44-L80) | E7.7 |
| [BRIN](../../../glossary.md#brin) | Neither | Only access path, always lossy | None | Opclass strategies; `IS [NOT] NULL` | [brin.c:254-290](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/brin/brin.c#L254-L290) | E7.8 |

Once eligible, index paths compete like every other path. `add_path` keeps a path unless another is at least as cheap and at least as good in ordering, parameterization and parallel safety ([chapter 5](#chapter-5-estimate-costs) and [chapter 8](#chapter-8-search-join-orders-and-methods)). That is why several paths for one index can survive: a cheap unordered bitmap path and a dearer ordered index path serve different parents.

| Feature | Eligible when | Rejected or weakened when | Measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multicolumn index | Any column may have a clause; B-tree searches the leading equality columns efficiently | A clause only on a later column means a whole-index scan, which usually costs more than the heap scan | E7.3: `Seq Scan` at 601.00; forced with `enable_seqscan = off` (a forced setting), the index-only path costs 693.30 |
| Ordering | Pathkeys match an `ORDER BY`, merge join or grouping need | The order is unused, so the pathkeys are truncated ([indxpath.c:913-921](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L913-L921)) | E7.3: `Index Scan Backward using orders_cust_time` for `customer_id = 7 ORDER BY ordered_at DESC LIMIT 3` |
| Distance ordering | `amcanorderbyop` and an ascending, NULLS LAST pathkey on `col <-> const` ([indxpath.c:3020-3060](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L3020-L3060)) | Descending order or a volatile expression | E7.6: `Order By: (p <-> '(500,500)'::point)` |
| Expression index | The query uses an identical expression | Any different expression, even an equivalent one | E7.9: `lower(email) = ...` uses the index; `email = ...` does not |
| Partial index | `predOK` for this query | A parameter instead of a constant; a different constant | E7.10 |
| Covering index | Every needed column is a key or `INCLUDE` column | A needed column is missing, or an expression is needed | E7.11: `Index Only Scan ... Heap Fetches: 0` |
| `= ANY (array)` | B-tree natively; other AMs only through a bitmap | `ALL`, or an array that references this table | E7.2: `Index Cond: (customer_id = ANY ('{500,501,502}'::integer[]))` |

In the 17 development cycle, `5bf748b86b` let B-tree scans with `= ANY` on a non-leading column keep their index order, and removed the planner's earlier workaround paths for that case. The current `get_index_paths()` accordingly skips only non-native `= ANY` clauses ([indxpath.c:710-767](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L710-L767)).

#### 7.6 Exceptions and limitations

| Condition or state | Behavior | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `indisvalid = false` | Index skipped entirely ([plancat.c:263-267](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L263-L267)) | E7.14: seq scan despite an index on `status` |
| `indcheckxmin` horizon not yet passed | Index skipped; plan marked transient ([plancat.c:269-281](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L269-L281)) | A cached plan is rebuilt once `TransactionXmin` moves |
| Clause collation differs from the index collation | No match ([indxpath.c:39-40](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L39-L40)) | E3.12: `COLLATE "C"` ignores a default-collation index even in a C database |
| Operator not in the column's opfamily and no support function | No match ([indxpath.c:2448-2458](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L2448-L2458)) | E7.5: `>` cannot use a hash index |
| Index side wrapped in an expression | No match unless an expression index stores the same expression ([indxpath.c#match_index_to_operand](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L3681-L3744)) | E7.2: `id + 0 = 42` is a seq scan |
| `LIKE` prefix on a non-C collation index without a pattern opclass | The support function returns no bounds ([like_support.c:428-437](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/like_support.c#L428-L437)) | Not measured here: this cluster uses C collation |
| Partial index and a query parameter | Predicate proof fails ([predtest.c:1842-1858](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/predtest.c#L1842-L1858)) | E7.10: the generic plan uses the full index |
| Update or lock target with a partial index | Implied quals stay in the plan ([indxpath.c:3317-3334](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L3317-L3334)) | Extra filter work, so EvalPlanQual can recheck |
| GIN with `enable_bitmapscan = off` | The bitmap path carries `disable_cost`, and GIN has no plain path to fall back to ([ginutil.c:79-80](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L79-L80), [costsize.c:1040-1041](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L1040-L1041)) | E7.7 (a forced setting): a seq scan wins |
| `enable_indexonlyscan = off` | No index-only path is built; plain index paths remain ([indxpath.c:1738-1740](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1738-L1740)) | No `disable_cost` involved |
| Partitioned index | No size and no cost estimator ([plancat.c:424-439](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L424-L439), [plancat.c:502-507](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L502-L507)) | Used only for proofs such as uniqueness; partitions' own indexes are scanned |
| Expression column in an index-only check | Ignored, so such an index cannot serve an index-only scan of the expression ([indxpath.c:1776-1785](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/indxpath.c#L1776-L1785)) | A plain index scan is used instead |
| Non-B-tree AM with `amcanorder` but no B-tree mapping of `<` | The index is treated as unordered ([plancat.c:407-414](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L407-L414)) | Relevant only to extension AMs |

#### 7.7 Formulas and worked examples

**LIMIT over an ordered index.** A `Limit` node charges its input's startup cost plus the input's run cost scaled by the fraction of rows it will fetch: `startup + (total - startup) x count / input_rows` ([pathnode.c:3910-3924](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/pathnode.c#L3910-L3924)). This is why an index that delivers rows in the wanted order wins small `LIMIT` queries even when a full scan of it is expensive.

| Input path, estimated | `count` | Derived Limit total | Estimated Limit, same run |
|---|---|---|---|
| E7.2 `Index Scan Backward` `0.29..1015.29 rows=30000` | 5 | `0.29 + 1015.00 x 5 / 30000 = 0.46` | `0.29..0.46` |
| E7.6 GiST `Order By` scan `0.28..1728.28 rows=20000` | 5 | `0.28 + 1728.00 x 5 / 20000 = 0.71` | `0.28..0.71` |

The quoted input costs are rounded to two decimals, so a derived figure can differ from the printed one by 0.01.

**BRIN recheck.** A BRIN bitmap adds whole block ranges as lossy pages ([brin.c:915-926](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/brin/brin.c#L915-L926)), 128 pages per range by default ([brin.h:39](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/brin.h#L39)). Its `Bitmap Index Scan` reports ten "rows" per page, because the AM knows pages, not rows ([brin.c:936-941](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/brin/brin.c#L936-L941)). Derived from E7.8:

1. Ranges read: `Heap Blocks: lossy=128`, one range.
2. Reported index rows: `128 x 10 = 1280`, matching `actual rows=1280`.
3. Heap rows examined: `1728 + 9536 = 11264` (matched plus `Rows Removed by Index Recheck`).
4. Rows per page: `600000 / 6819 = 88.0` (E12.1 sizes), and `128 x 88 = 11264`.

So one day of `events` (1,728 rows) cost a scan of one full 128-page range.

**Why the full-index path lost.** In E7.3 the only index was `(customer_id, ordered_at)` and the query filtered on `ordered_at` alone. With the default settings the plan was a `Seq Scan` costing `601.00`. With `enable_seqscan = off` (a forced setting) the same query produced `Index Only Scan using orders_cust_time ... cost=0.29..693.30`. The index path was eligible all along; it lost by `693.30 - 601.00 = 92.30` cost units, because it must read the entire index to find one timestamp.

#### 7.8 Planning versus execution

| Decision | Made by the planner | Made or adapted by the executor |
|---|---|---|
| Which index and which conditions | Fixed in the plan ([createplan.c:3050-3090](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/createplan.c#L3050-L3090)) | Never changed |
| Heap visits for an index-only scan | Priced from the stored all-visible fraction | Decided per index entry from the live visibility map ([nodeIndexonlyscan.c:161-169](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeIndexonlyscan.c#L161-L169)); E6.3 made 3,060 heap fetches after an update |
| Lossy bitmap pages | Assumed: every row is charged a recheck ([costsize.c:1073-1085](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L1073-L1085)) | The bitmap becomes lossy when it outgrows `work_mem`, or always for BRIN; E7.8 rechecked 11,264 rows |
| Parameterized index conditions | The expression `customer_id = c.id` | The value comes from each outer row; E7.13 ran the inner scan with `loops=5` |
| `= ANY` on a B-tree | One path, one index condition | nbtree decides how many descents to make and when to skip ahead (`5bf748b86b`) |
| Invalid or not-yet-ready indexes | Excluded from planning | Still maintained on insert if `indisready` ([plancat.c:256-262](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L256-L262)) |

#### 7.9 Lifecycle

| Event | State before | State after | Effect on later planning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CREATE INDEX` commits | No index | Valid index in the relcache | Every later planning run sees it; cached plans on the table are invalidated ([chapter 14](#chapter-14-build-cache-and-invalidate-plans), E14.4) |
| `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` fails | Build in progress | `indisvalid = false` left behind (E7.14) | Ignored by the planner until dropped or rebuilt |
| Index built while old snapshots can see broken HOT chains | `indcheckxmin` set | Usable once the horizon passes | Plans made meanwhile are transient ([plancat.c:269-281](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L269-L281)) |
| Index grows or shrinks | Old file size | New `pages` at the next planning run ([plancat.c:473-477](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L473-L477)) | Cost moves without `ANALYZE` |
| `ANALYZE` after creating an expression index | No statistics for the expression | Expression statistics stored | Selectivity of the expression improves; see E4.14 in [chapter 4](#chapter-4-estimate-rows-and-widths) |
| `VACUUM` | Visibility-map bits cleared by writes | Bits set; `relallvisible` updated | Index-only scans stop visiting the heap (E6.3) |
| Query switches from a constant to a parameter | Partial index proven | Proof fails in the generic plan | A different index is chosen (E7.10) |
| An extension sets `get_relation_info_hook` | Real indexes only | Hypothetical entries possible | Plans can be priced for indexes that do not exist |

#### 7.10 Regression coverage and gaps

- AM and index property reporting: [amutils.sql:1-30](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/amutils.sql#L1-L30).
- B-tree partial indexes: [create_index.sql:54-62](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/create_index.sql#L54-L62); `IS NULL` on GiST: [create_index.sql:168-182](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/create_index.sql#L168-L182); `= ANY` combinations: [create_index.sql:797-804](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/create_index.sql#L797-L804).
- `LIKE` prefix index conditions: [btree_index.sql:152-166](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/btree_index.sql#L152-L166).
- Range containment simplification (`075df6b208`): [rangetypes.sql:650-665](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/rangetypes.sql#L650-L665).
- Hash index plans: [hash_index.sql:126](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/hash_index.sql#L126). GiST nearest-neighbour ordering: [gist.sql:68-82](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/gist.sql#L68-L82). GIN plans: [gin.sql:39-47](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/gin.sql#L39-L47). BRIN plans: [brin.sql:470](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/brin.sql#L470). Covering indexes: [index_including.sql:231](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/regress/sql/index_including.sql#L231).
- Predicate proofs, directly: the `test_predtest` module ([test_predtest/README:1-12](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/test/modules/test_predtest/README#L1-L12)).
- **Gap: `indcheckxmin` and transient plans.** No experiment on this page creates an index while an old snapshot is open; the behavior is cited from source only.
- **Gap: non-C collations.** The cluster was initialized with `--locale=C` and built without ICU, so the `LIKE` fallback for non-C index collations and nondeterministic collations were not measured.

#### 7.11 Causal summary

1. Initial state: the valid, visible indexes; `get_relation_info` copies their columns, operator families, collations and AM flags.
2. Transformation: partial-index predicates are proven against this query's constants, and each clause is matched literally (same key, same collation, operator in the family) or through a support function.
3. Output: matches, useful orderings and index-only possibilities become index and bitmap paths, routed by AM capability.
4. Interaction: the AM estimators and the heap-visit model price them, and `add_path` keeps the survivors.
5. Observed result: the executor still decides heap visits, bitmap lossiness and array descents.
6. Refresh: a new index, a failed build, a `VACUUM` or a switch to parameters changes the next plan.

### Chapter 8. Search join orders and methods

#### 8.1 Main idea

A query that joins several tables can be answered by many join trees, and each join in a tree can use one of three methods. The planner does not enumerate whole trees. It builds one RelOptInfo for every set of tables it might join, bottom up: first all useful pairs, then all useful triples, and so on. For each set it tries the three methods in both input orders and keeps only the paths that no other path beats ([optimizer/README#Join-Tree-Construction](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/README#L124-L170)).

This is a [join order search](../../../glossary.md#join-order-search) by dynamic programming. It is exhaustive only within one list of items to join, and two settings decide how long those lists get: `join_collapse_limit` for written `JOIN`s and `from_collapse_limit` for `FROM` lists. When one list reaches `geqo_threshold` items, the planner switches to the genetic search, [GEQO](../../../glossary.md#geqo), which samples join orders instead of trying them all ([allpaths.c#make_rel_from_joinlist-search](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3372-L3377)).

Two results surprise most readers. Twelve tables joined by eleven explicit `JOIN`s never reach GEQO at default settings, because the written joins are cut into lists of at most eight (E8.9). And a semi join from `EXISTS` may run as an ordinary inner join after one side is made unique (E8.6). The chapter uses E8.1 to E8.10, with E4.8b, E5.9 and E7.13 as supporting evidence; [E8.1](#measurement-script) is Q2.

#### 8.2 Values and structures

| Value or structure | Meaning | Where it comes from | Current state, stored state, estimate or parameter | Used later by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| joinlist | Items to be joined in any order; an item is a table or a nested sub-list planned separately ([initsplan.c#deconstruct_jointree-joinlist](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L731-L737)) | `deconstruct_jointree()` while it files quals (chapter 3) | current, derived from the query and two parameters | `make_rel_from_joinlist()` |
| `join_collapse_limit`, `from_collapse_limit` | The largest list that written `JOIN`s or `FROM` items are merged into ([initsplan.c#deconstruct_recurse-from-collapse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L862-L893), [initsplan.c#deconstruct_recurse-join-collapse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L1066-L1097)) | settings, default 8 each ([guc_tables.c#join_collapse_limit](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2094-L2105), [guc_tables.c#from_collapse_limit](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2081-L2092)) | parameter | the shape of the joinlist |
| `levels_needed` | Number of items in one joinlist, which is the depth of the search ([allpaths.c#make_rel_from_joinlist-levels](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3312-L3320)) | length of the joinlist | current | the choice between exhaustive search and GEQO |
| `geqo`, `geqo_threshold`, `geqo_effort` | Whether and when to switch to GEQO, and how hard it searches ([guc_tables.c#geqo_threshold](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2107-L2115), [guc_tables.c#geqo_effort](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2117-L2125)) | settings: on, 12, 5 (measured, E8.9 and E16.1; [geqo.h:55](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/optimizer/geqo.h#L55)) | parameter | `make_rel_from_joinlist()`, `gimme_pool_size()` |
| `join_rel_level[k]` | All join relations of exactly `k` items found so far ([allpaths.c#standard_join_search-levels](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3423-L3446)) | `standard_join_search()` | current, for this search only | the next level of the search |
| join `RelOptInfo` | One relation per set of joined tables, shared by every way of building that set ([relnode.c#build_join_rel-reuse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/relnode.c#L679-L697)) | `build_join_rel()` | its row estimate is computed once, when the set is first built ([relnode.c#build_join_rel-size](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/relnode.c#L822-L826)) | every path of that set |
| `SpecialJoinInfo` | An outer, semi, anti or full join with the minimum sets of tables required on each side ([pathnodes.h#SpecialJoinInfo](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/nodes/pathnodes.h#L2892-L2911)) | built during qual distribution (chapter 3) | current | `join_is_legal()` |
| `JoinPathExtraData` | Per-pair facts shared by all methods: whether the inner side is provably unique, mergeable clauses, semi-join correction factors, allowed parameter sources ([joinpath.c#add_paths_to_joinrel-inner-unique](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L155-L201), [joinpath.c#add_paths_to_joinrel-clauses-factors](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L210-L226), [joinpath.c#add_paths_to_joinrel-param-sources](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L229-L276)) | `add_paths_to_joinrel()` | current, estimates for the factors | every `try_*_path()` |

#### 8.3 Logic map

```text
query_planner: deconstruct_jointree                                    [A]
  FROM list: merge items while the list stays <= from_collapse_limit
  written JOIN: merge both sides while <= join_collapse_limit;
                FULL JOIN is never merged
  -> joinlist (items may be nested sub-lists)
make_one_rel -> make_rel_from_joinlist (recurses into each sub-list)    [B]
  levels_needed = items in this list
  1 item? ---------------------------------> that relation, done
  join_search_hook set? -------------------> the extension decides
  geqo on and levels_needed >= geqo_threshold? -> GEQO               [C]
  otherwise standard_join_search:
    for level = 2 .. levels_needed: join_search_one_level           [D]
      level-1 relations x single items, where a join clause or an
        order restriction links them; a relation with neither is
        tried against every item (Cartesian product)
      bushy pairs (k items x level-k items), only with a clause
      nothing found? last-ditch Cartesian products
      each candidate pair -> make_join_rel                         [E]
        join_is_legal (SpecialJoinInfos)? no -> pair rejected
        build_join_rel: reuse or create the set's RelOptInfo
        populate_joinrel_with_paths: both input orders, per join type
          add_paths_to_joinrel                                      [F]
            inner provably unique? mergeable clauses? hashable clauses?
            1 merge join with explicit sorts
            2 nested loops (plain, Material, Memoize, parameterized)
              and merge joins on presorted outer paths
            4 hash joins (and parallel hash)
            5 FDW join pushdown   6 set_join_pathlist_hook
            each candidate: cheap cost bound -> add_path_precheck
                            -> full path -> add_path             [G]
    after each level: partitionwise and Gather paths, set_cheapest  [H]
  -> the relation of all tables, handed to grouping_planner
```

- [A] [initsplan.c#deconstruct_recurse-from-collapse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L862-L893), [initsplan.c#deconstruct_recurse-join-collapse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L1066-L1097)
- [B] [allpaths.c#make_rel_from_joinlist](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3306-L3377)
- [C] [geqo_main.c#geqo](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_main.c#L101-L124), [geqo_eval.c#geqo_eval-fitness](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L101-L118)
- [D] [joinrels.c#join_search_one_level-linear](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L91-L137), [joinrels.c#join_search_one_level-bushy](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L141-L197), [joinrels.c#join_search_one_level-last-ditch](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L201-L232)
- [E] [joinrels.c#make_join_rel](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L722-L779), [joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L916-L948), [joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths-semi-anti](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L975-L1047)
- [F] [joinpath.c#add_paths_to_joinrel-methods](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L278-L345)
- [G] [joinpath.c#try_nestloop_path-precheck](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L802-L834)
- [H] [allpaths.c#standard_join_search-per-level](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3437-L3481)

#### 8.4 Step by step

##### Step 1: turn the join tree into lists

Input: the query's join tree after chapter 3's transformations. `deconstruct_recurse()` walks it. For a `FROM` list it merges each child's items into one list while that list, plus one item for each sibling still to come, stays within `from_collapse_limit`; it always merges one-item children ([initsplan.c#deconstruct_recurse-from-collapse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L862-L893)).

For a written `JOIN` it merges the two sides' lists only while their combined length stays within `join_collapse_limit`. Otherwise it keeps them as two items. A `FULL JOIN` is never merged, so its join order is fixed ([initsplan.c#deconstruct_recurse-join-collapse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L1066-L1097)).

Output: a joinlist, possibly with sub-lists. Consequence: each list is searched separately, so the limits trade plan quality for planning effort. E8.8 shows the extreme: with `join_collapse_limit = 1`, the written order `(items JOIN orders) JOIN customers` is kept and costs 2902.66, against 788.08 when the planner may reorder (Estimated, E8.8, forced setting).

##### Step 2: pick the search strategy

`make_rel_from_joinlist()` counts the items in its list and plans every sub-list recursively, treating each result as one item. A `join_search_hook` takes over if an extension set one. Otherwise GEQO runs when `geqo` is on and the list has at least `geqo_threshold` items; else `standard_join_search()` runs ([allpaths.c#make_rel_from_joinlist-recurse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3327-L3377)).

The count is per list, not per query. That is why E8.9a, twelve tables joined by eleven written `JOIN`s, never reaches GEQO: the collapse rule splits them into lists of eight and five items (derived below). The documentation states the same interaction from the other side: raising either collapse limit to `geqo_threshold` or more may trigger GEQO ([config.sgml#guc-from-collapse-limit](../../../../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L6397-L6399), [config.sgml#guc-join-collapse-limit](../../../../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L6449-L6451)).

##### Step 3: enumerate candidate pairs, level by level

`standard_join_search()` starts with the single items at level 1 and asks `join_search_one_level()` for each higher level ([allpaths.c#standard_join_search-levels](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3423-L3446)). It first joins each relation of the previous level to single items it is linked to by a join clause, an equivalence class or an order restriction. A relation with no such link is joined to every item, which is a Cartesian product ([joinrels.c#join_search_one_level-linear](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L91-L137)).

It then tries bushy pairs, such as two two-table joins, but only when `have_relevant_joinclause()` or `have_join_order_restriction()` links them ([joinrels.c#join_search_one_level-bushy](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L141-L197)). If a level produced nothing, it falls back to Cartesian products ([joinrels.c#join_search_one_level-last-ditch](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L201-L232)). This clause-driven rule is what keeps the search smaller than the full factorial.

##### Step 4: check legality

`make_join_rel()` first asks `join_is_legal()` whether the pair may be joined at all ([joinrels.c#make_join_rel-legal](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L722-L729)). The answer comes from the query's `SpecialJoinInfo`s. Each records the minimum sets of tables that must sit on each side of an outer join, a semi or anti join, or a full join ([pathnodes.h#SpecialJoinInfo-comment](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/include/nodes/pathnodes.h#L2803-L2831)).

The rules come from three outer-join identities: some joins may move into or out of an outer join's left side, but not freely into its nullable side ([optimizer/README#Valid-OUTER-JOIN-Optimizations](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/README#L193-L254)). An illegal pair gets no relation at all, so no path of that shape exists.

`join_is_legal()` also enforces `LATERAL` references. A side that references the other must become the inner input of a nested loop, so references in both directions reject the pair ([joinrels.c#join_is_legal-lateral](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L548-L605)).

##### Step 5: one relation per set of tables

`build_join_rel()` looks up the `RelOptInfo` for the pair's set of tables and creates it only the first time ([relnode.c#build_join_rel-reuse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/relnode.c#L679-L697)). The set's row estimate is computed then, once ([relnode.c#build_join_rel-size](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/relnode.c#L822-L826)). So `{orders, customers}` has one row count, whichever pair built it; chapter 4 explains how that count is estimated.

##### Step 6: generate method paths for both input orders

`populate_joinrel_with_paths()` calls `add_paths_to_joinrel()` once per input order and join type. An inner or full join is tried both ways. A left join is also tried as a right join with the inputs swapped, and an anti join as a right anti join. A semi join is also tried as an inner join with its right side de-duplicated, on either side ([joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L916-L948), [joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths-semi-anti](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L975-L1047)).

`add_paths_to_joinrel()` then generates the method paths in a fixed order: merge joins that sort both inputs, nested loops and merge joins over presorted outer paths, and hash joins. Last, a foreign data wrapper may add a pushed-down join and an extension may add or remove paths through `set_join_pathlist_hook` ([joinpath.c#add_paths_to_joinrel-methods](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L278-L345)).

For nested loops, `match_unsorted_outer()` pairs each outer path with the cheapest inner path for each parameterization, the unparameterized one included, with a [Memoize](../../../glossary.md#memoize) version of each, and with a materialized copy of the cheapest inner path ([joinpath.c#match_unsorted_outer-nestloops](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L1848-L1897)). The parameterized path case is the index lookup per outer row that chapter 7 builds (E7.13).

##### Step 7: compare and keep

Each `try_*_path()` first computes a cheap lower bound on cost and asks `add_path_precheck()` whether an existing path already beats it. Only then does it build the full path and call `add_path()` ([joinpath.c#try_nestloop_path-precheck](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L802-L834)). After a whole level is built, the planner adds partitionwise and Gather paths and records each relation's cheapest paths ([allpaths.c#standard_join_search-per-level](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3437-L3481)).

Output: a relation for all tables whose surviving paths go to `grouping_planner()`. Consequence: grouping and sorting are planned only on top of these surviving paths, using the cheapest one or a presorted one when that is cheaper than sorting ([optimizer/README#Join-Tree-Construction-final](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/README#L180-L182)).

##### Step 8: the genetic search

GEQO treats a join order as a tour through the items. It seeds a pool of random tours, ranks each by the cheapest total cost of the plan `gimme_tree()` builds from it, and breeds new tours for a fixed number of generations ([geqo_main.c#geqo](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_main.c#L101-L124), [geqo_main.c#geqo-loop](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_main.c#L183-L186), [geqo_eval.c#geqo_eval-fitness](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L101-L118)).

`gimme_tree()` follows the tour but postpones joins that are illegal or lack a join clause, which lets it build bushy trees ([geqo_eval.c#gimme_tree-comment](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L153-L160), [geqo_eval.c#desirable_join](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L324-L338)). Each evaluation builds its join relations in a private memory context and deletes it afterwards ([geqo_eval.c#geqo_eval-context](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L66-L78), [geqo_eval.c:128-130](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L128-L130)), so those relations do not accumulate, which fits GEQO's lower planner memory in E8.9. The seed comes from `geqo_seed`, so the same query with the same settings and statistics gets the same plan every time ([geqo_main.c#geqo-seed](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_main.c#L105-L106)).

#### 8.5 Eligibility and comparison

| Method | Eligible when | Not eligible when | Comparison notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nested loop | Any join clause, or none; inner, left, semi and anti joins ([joinpath.c#match_unsorted_outer-jointypes](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L1732-L1762)) | right, right-anti and full joins | The only method that can pass outer values into a parameterized inner index scan (E7.13); hash joins reject such inner paths ([joinpath.c#hash_inner_and_outer-param](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L2149-L2156)) |
| Nested loop with Materialize | `enable_material` on and the inner path does not already materialize ([joinpath.c#match_unsorted_outer-material](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L1788-L1798)) | the inner path is parameterized by the outer side ([joinpath.c#match_unsorted_outer-param](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L1767-L1773)) | Each rescan costs `cpu_operator_cost` per stored row ([costsize.c#cost_rescan-material](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4604-L4615)) |
| Nested loop with Memoize | `enable_memoize` on; at least two outer rows; the inner path has parameter clauses or lateral references; hashable cache keys; no volatile functions on the inner side ([joinpath.c#get_memoize_path-gates](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L591-L626), [joinpath.c#get_memoize_path-volatile-hashops](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L660-L713)) | semi and anti joins, because `add_paths_to_joinrel()` never marks their inner side unique ([joinpath.c#add_paths_to_joinrel-inner-unique](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L155-L201)); a unique inner join whose inner path covers only part of the join clauses ([joinpath.c#get_memoize_path-unique-partial](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L627-L657)) | Rescan cost falls with the expected hit ratio (formula below) |
| Merge join | At least one mergejoinable clause, from an operator with a B-tree family ([initsplan.c#check_mergejoinable](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L3374-L3398), [joinpath.c#select_mergejoin_clauses](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L2374-L2426)) | right, right-anti and full joins with any other join clause | Sorted inputs come from an index or an explicit sort; fast start when both are presorted (E8.3) |
| Hash join | At least one hashjoinable clause ([joinpath.c#hash_inner_and_outer-clauses](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L2105-L2135)) | no hashable equality | Tries the cheapest-startup and cheapest-total outer paths against the cheapest-total inner ([joinpath.c#hash_inner_and_outer-paths](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L2139-L2147)) |
| Parallel hash | the outer and inner sides both have partial paths, `enable_parallel_hash` on ([joinpath.c#hash_inner_and_outer-parallel](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L2258-L2290)) | right, right-anti and full joins for the non-shared variant ([joinpath.c#hash_inner_and_outer-parallel-safe](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L2296-L2310)) | Chapter 12 |
| Unique-ified semi join | the semi join's operators can sort or hash, and one input is exactly the semi join's right side ([joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths-semi](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L975-L1021)) | the right side cannot be de-duplicated | Competes with the plain semi join by cost (E8.6 against E8.7) |

The `enable_*` switches for join methods act in two different ways. `enable_nestloop = off` keeps nested-loop paths but adds `disable_cost` at final costing, so a nested loop can still win when nothing else is legal ([costsize.c#final_cost_nestloop-disable](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L3342-L3348)). `enable_mergejoin = off` and `enable_hashjoin = off` stop merge and hash paths from being generated at all ([joinpath.c#add_paths_to_joinrel-mergeclauses](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L204-L217), [joinpath.c:321](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L321)).

The exception is a full join, which may have no other method. For it, merge and hash paths are still generated when their switches are off, and their final costing adds `disable_cost` instead ([costsize.c:3794](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L3794), [costsize.c:4224](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4224)). Likewise `enable_memoize = off` and `enable_material = off` prevent Memoize and optional Material inner paths from being built ([joinpath.c#get_memoize_path-enable](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L591-L593), [joinpath.c#match_unsorted_outer-material](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L1788-L1798)).

`add_path()` rejects a path of a joinrel when another path dominates it. The other path must be at least as cheap in startup and total cost, within a 1 % fuzz, and at least as well sorted. It must also return no more rows, need no more outer relations, and be at least as parallel-safe ([pathnode.c#add_path](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/pathnode.c#L361-L373), [pathnode.c#compare_path_costs_fuzzily](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/pathnode.c#L164-L215)). So a merge join can survive against a cheaper hash join when its sorted output is useful higher up, as in E8.3.

#### 8.6 Exceptions and limitations

| Condition or state | Behavior | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| A `FULL JOIN` whose clauses are neither mergejoinable nor hashable | error "FULL JOIN is only supported with merge-joinable or hash-joinable join conditions" ([joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths-full](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L949-L974)) | the query cannot be planned at all |
| A proposed pair joins part of a special join's minimum right side to tables outside it, without performing that join | `join_is_legal()` rejects it, unless both inputs already overlap that right side or the pair can move into the right side of a strict `LEFT JOIN` ([joinrels.c#join_is_legal-rhs-violation](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L491-L546)) | fewer join orders; some queries only have bushy legal plans |
| A level finds no pair with a clause | Cartesian products are forced ([joinrels.c#join_search_one_level-last-ditch](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L201-L232)) | the search continues; with special joins a level may stay empty until a bushy join at a later level succeeds, and without special joins or `LATERAL` an empty level is an internal error ([joinrels.c#join_search_one_level-empty-level](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L234-L255)) |
| An inner join's input is provably empty, or its qual is constant false | the join is marked dummy: zero rows and one empty `Append` path ([joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths-inner](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L916-L931), [joinrels.c#mark_dummy_rel](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L1393-L1406)); outer and anti joins can instead mark only their nullable side dummy ([joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L932-L948), [joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths-anti](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L1023-L1039)) | the plan shows a `Result` with a false one-time filter ([createplan.c#create_append_plan-dummy](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/createplan.c#L1245-L1253)) |
| The inner side's most common join key would overflow hash memory on its own | `disable_cost` is added to the hash join ([costsize.c#final_cost_hashjoin-mcv](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4313-L4324)) | another method wins unless none is possible, because batching cannot split equal keys |
| One side of a pair has a `LATERAL` reference to the other | allowed only as a nested loop with the referencing side inside; references in both directions, indirect references, or a special join such a nested loop cannot implement reject the pair ([joinrels.c#join_is_legal-lateral](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L548-L605)) | the referencing side always runs as a parameterized inner input |
| GEQO cannot form one tree from a tour | `gimme_tree()` returns nothing and the tour gets infinite cost ([geqo_eval.c#geqo_eval-fitness](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L101-L118)) | if even the best tour fails, error "geqo failed to make a valid plan" ([geqo_main.c:274-275](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_main.c#L274-L275)) |
| GEQO and fractional results | GEQO ranks tours by total cost only, ignoring LIMIT fractions and parameterized paths ([geqo_eval.c#geqo_eval-total-cost-only](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L104-L110)) | a fast-start plan can be missed |
| A nested loop input path parameterized by the outer join being formed at this join | rejected ([joinpath.c#try_nestloop_path](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L738-L747)) | the parameter would come from a join that is not yet complete, so that input path cannot be used at this join |

#### 8.7 Formulas and worked examples

##### Q2: why hash joins (E8.1, E8.2)

Q2 joins pending orders to their items and customers. The planner estimated 9057 joined rows and 4 groups; the run produced exactly 9057 and 4 (Measured, E8.1):

```text
 HashAggregate  (cost=2553.06..2553.11 rows=4 width=45) (actual rows=4 loops=1)
...
   ->  Hash Join  (cost=705.74..2439.85 rows=9057 width=15) (actual rows=9057 loops=1)
         Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
         ->  Hash Join  (cost=638.74..2349.02 rows=9057 width=14) (actual rows=9057 loops=1)
               Hash Cond: (i.order_id = o.id)
               ->  Seq Scan on items i  (cost=0.00..1474.00 rows=90000 width=14) (actual rows=90000 loops=1)
               ->  Hash  (cost=601.00..601.00 rows=3019 width=8) (actual rows=3019 loops=1)
...
         ->  Hash  (cost=42.00..42.00 rows=2000 width=9) (actual rows=2000 loops=1)
```

A hash join's startup cost is the inner input's total cost plus, per inner row, one hash computation per hash clause and one `cpu_tuple_cost` to insert the row ([costsize.c#initial_cost_hashjoin-startup](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4092-L4108)):

| Join | Inner total cost | Inner rows x (0.0025 + 0.01) | Plus outer startup | Derived startup | Plan |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| items with pending orders | 601.00 | 3019 x 0.0125 = 37.74 | 0 | 638.74 | 638.74 |
| that result with customers | 42.00 | 2000 x 0.0125 = 25.00 | 638.74 | 705.74 | 705.74 |

E8.2 prices the same items-orders join with each method in turn (Estimated, E8.2, forced settings):

| Method | Plan | Startup | Total | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hash join | chosen by default | 638.74 | 2349.02 | one pass over each input |
| Merge join (`enable_hashjoin = off`) | index scan on `items_pkey` and a sort of 3019 orders | 775.79 | 4777.52 | reads all 90,000 items in key order; startup is the two inputs' startups, 0.29 + 775.50 ([costsize.c#initial_cost_mergejoin-outer](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L3660-L3666), [costsize.c#initial_cost_mergejoin-inner-sort](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L3669-L3685)) |
| Nested loop (both others off) | 3019 index lookups into `items_pkey` | 0.29 | 5021.12 | 3019 inner scans at 1.43 each |

The hash join wins because its total cost is lowest and nothing above it needs sorted rows.

##### A fast start for LIMIT (E8.3)

With `ORDER BY o.id LIMIT 20`, both inputs are read in key order from index-only scans and merged. The merge join's own total cost is 4328.58, above the 2611.28 that E8.8 prices for a hash join of the same two tables, but the limit reads only 20 of 90,000 rows. `Limit` charges the fraction 20/90000 of the run cost: 0.58 + (4328.58 - 0.58) x 20 / 90000 = 1.54, the plan's figure (Estimated, E8.3; [pathnode.c#adjust_limit_rows_costs](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/pathnode.c#L3881-L3924)). This path survives `add_path()` because it has the cheapest startup and useful sort order.

##### Materialize in a nested loop (E8.5)

The join clause `o.amount > c.id` is neither hashable nor mergeable, so only a nested loop can run it. The inner side, 30 expensive orders, is materialized once and rescanned 2000 times (Estimated, E8.5):

```text
...
   ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.00..1693.07 rows=20000 width=0)
         Join Filter: (orders.amount > (c.id)::numeric)
         ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (cost=0.00..42.00 rows=2000 width=4)
         ->  Materialize  (cost=0.00..601.15 rows=30 width=6)
               ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..601.00 rows=30 width=6)
```

| Term | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Material first scan | 601.00 + 2 x 0.0025 x 30 = 601.15 | [costsize.c#cost_material](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L2453-L2476) |
| 1999 rescans | 1999 x 0.0025 x 30 = 149.93 | [costsize.c#cost_rescan-material](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4604-L4615) |
| Join filter and tuple cost | (0.01 + 0.0025 + 0.0025) x 2000 x 30 = 900.00, the cast and the comparison at one `cpu_operator_cost` each | [costsize.c#final_cost_nestloop-cpu](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L3462-L3473) |
| Outer scan | 42.00 | plan |
| Derived total | 42.00 + 601.15 + 149.93 + 900.00 = 1693.08, against 1693.07 in the plan | outer, first inner scan and rescans added by [costsize.c#initial_cost_nestloop-sum](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L3253-L3288); the 0.01 gap is rounding of the printed inputs |

The CPU charge counts every candidate pair, 2000 x 30, not the 20,000 estimated output rows ([costsize.c#final_cost_nestloop-cpu](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L3462-L3473)).

##### Memoize: estimated against measured hits (E8.4)

E8.4 joins 6000 order lines to every line with the same product, serially so that its counters repeat (forced setting). The inner side is an index-only scan parameterized by `a.product_id`, cached by Memoize (Measured, E8.4):

```text
...
         ->  Memoize  (cost=0.30..3.51 rows=180 width=4) (actual rows=2296 loops=6000)
               Cache Key: a.product_id
               Cache Mode: logical
               Hits: 5505  Misses: 495  Evictions: 0  Overflows: 0  Memory Usage: 3183kB
...
```

The planner estimates the hit ratio as `(calls - ndistinct) / calls`, times the fraction of keys the cache can hold ([costsize.c#cost_memoize_rescan-hit-ratio](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L2549-L2599)). Here `calls` is 6000 outer rows. The `schema` stage draws every line's product from 1 to 500 (see [Measurement Script](#measurement-script)), so `ndistinct` is at most 500.

The cache can hold every key. One entry stores 180 rows at 32 bytes each, plus 16 bytes of bookkeeping per row, 48 per entry and the 4-byte key: 5,760 + 2,880 + 48 + 4 = 8,692 bytes on this 64-bit build. Hash memory, 4MB x `hash_mem_multiplier` 2 = 8 MB (E16.1), therefore holds floor(8,388,608 / 8,692) = 965 entries ([nodeMemoize.c#MemoizeTuple-MemoizeEntry](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeMemoize.c#L94-L123), [costsize.c#cost_memoize_rescan-entry-size](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L2529-L2546), [nodeMemoize.c#ExecEstimateCacheEntryOverheadBytes](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeMemoize.c#L1172-L1176)). The derived hit ratio is therefore at least (6000 - 500) / 6000 = 0.917. The executor measured 5505 / 6000 = 0.9175, because 495 distinct products occurred.

Each rescan is priced at 3.50 x (1 - 0.9167) = 0.29 for the expected misses, plus 0.0025 for the lookup and 0.01 + 0.0025 x 180 = 0.46 for storing the entry, 0.754 in all ([costsize.c#cost_memoize_rescan-total](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L2599-L2620)). Eviction adds nothing, because 965 entries hold all 500 keys.

The nested loop adds the outer scan, the first inner scan and 5999 rescans ([costsize.c#initial_cost_nestloop-sum](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L3253-L3288)), then 0.01 per candidate pair. The derived total is 763.79 + 3.51 + 5999 x 0.754 + 0.01 x 6000 x 180 = 16,091 (rounded), within 0.02 % of the plan's 16089.13; the gap comes from the two-decimal inputs. Without Memoize the estimate is 32534.79 (Estimated, E8.4, forced setting).

##### Batching a hash join (E8.10)

At the default `work_mem`, the 28,491 non-cancelled orders fit in one batch; at 64kB they need 16 (Measured, E8.10, forced setting):

Default `work_mem` (4MB):

```text
...
   ->  Hash Join  (cost=957.14..2667.42 rows=85473 width=0) (actual rows=85473 loops=1)
...
               Buckets: 32768  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 1258kB
...
```

`work_mem = '64kB'`:

```text
...
   ->  Hash Join  (cost=1069.14..3595.42 rows=85473 width=0) (actual rows=85473 loops=1)
...
               Buckets: 4096  Batches: 16  Memory Usage: 96kB
...
```

When more than one batch is planned, the cost adds one sequential page write per inner page to startup and, to run cost, the inner pages read back plus the outer pages written and read ([costsize.c#initial_cost_hashjoin-batches](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4146-L4155)). Pages come from `page_size()`: rows x (8-byte aligned width + 24-byte tuple header) / 8192, rounded up ([costsize.c#relation_byte_size](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L6359-L6373)). The hash-qual CPU term stays the same, because bucket size is estimated over buckets x batches: 4096 x 16 = 65,536 and 32,768 x 1 both exceed the 28,491 distinct inner keys ([costsize.c#final_cost_hashjoin-virtualbuckets](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4233-L4234), [selfuncs.c#estimate_hash_bucket_stats-fraction](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/selfuncs.c#L3899-L3906)).

| Term | Calculation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Inner pages | 28491 x (8 + 24) / 8192 = 111.3, rounded up | 112 |
| Outer pages | 90000 x (8 + 24) / 8192 = 351.6, rounded up | 352 |
| Extra startup | 112 x `seq_page_cost` 1.0 | 112.00; 957.14 + 112 = 1069.14 |
| Extra run cost | 112 + 2 x 352 | 816.00 |
| Extra total | 112 + 816 = 928; 2667.42 + 928 = 3595.42 | matches the plan |

The executor printed `Batches: 16` without an "originally" figure, so the batch count it computed from the plan's row estimate never had to grow ([explain.c#show_hash_info-originally](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/explain.c#L3300-L3319)).

##### Twelve tables three ways (E8.9)

The twelve tables `j01` to `j12` form a chain of joins with 1000 rows each. The same query was planned three ways (costs estimated, planner memory measured, E8.9):

| Variant | Join lists | Search | Top cost | Planner memory used |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E8.9a: eleven written `JOIN`s, defaults | one list of 8 and one of 5 items (derived below) | dynamic programming in each list | 304.53 | 409kB |
| E8.9b: one `FROM` list, defaults | one list of 12 | GEQO, because 12 >= `geqo_threshold` | 310.29 | 163kB |
| E8.9c: one `FROM` list, `geqo = off` (forced setting) | one list of 12 | dynamic programming | 304.53 | 799kB |

Derivation of E8.9a's lists, from the `JOIN` rule in Step 1: the left-deep chain merges `j01` to `j08` into one list of 8. Joining `j09` would make 9 > 8, so the result becomes two items, `[j01..j08]` and `j09`. Adding `j10`, `j11` and `j12` gives lists of 3, 4 and 5 items, all within the limit. No list reaches 12, so GEQO never runs ([initsplan.c#deconstruct_recurse-join-collapse](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L1066-L1097)).

GEQO's effort follows from the defaults: the pool size is 2^(12+1) = 8192, capped at 50 x `geqo_effort` = 250, and the number of generations equals the pool size, 250 ([geqo_main.c#gimme_pool_size](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_main.c#L319-L358)). Here GEQO found a plan 1.9 % dearer than the exhaustive search, with a fifth of its memory.

#### 8.8 Planning versus execution

| Decided while planning | Decided or adapted while running |
|---|---|
| Join order, method, and which side is inner ([joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L916-L948), [joinrels.c#populate_joinrel_with_paths-semi-anti](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinrels.c#L975-L1047)) | nothing: the executor builds one state node per plan node and runs that tree as planned ([execProcnode.c#ExecInitNode](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/execProcnode.c#L126-L138)) |
| The hash join's estimated batch count and its disk cost ([costsize.c#initial_cost_hashjoin-size-batches](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4129-L4155)) | the executor recomputes the table size from the plan's row estimate and doubles the batch count whenever the table outgrows its memory ([nodeHash.c#ExecHashTableCreate-size](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeHash.c#L457-L470), [nodeHash.c#ExecHashTableInsert-grow](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeHash.c#L1691-L1698), [nodeHash.c#ExecHashIncreaseNumBatches](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeHash.c#L916-L935)) |
| The hash join cost assumes the skew optimization may be used, without pricing it ([costsize.c#initial_cost_hashjoin-size](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4120-L4137)) | the executor reads the outer key's most-common-values statistics and keeps the inner rows matching those values in memory ([nodeHash.c#ExecHashBuildSkewHash](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeHash.c#L2373-L2384)) |
| Memoize's expected number of cache entries ([costsize.c#cost_memoize_rescan-hit-ratio](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L2549-L2599)) | the cache evicts entries when it exceeds its memory limit ([nodeMemoize.c#cache_lookup-evict](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeMemoize.c#L577-L586)); E8.4 had none |
| Merge join's need to back up the inner input | the executor marks and restores the inner position, unless the planner set it to skip that ([nodeMergejoin.c:1195-1196](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeMergejoin.c#L1195-L1196), [nodeMergejoin.c:1081-1083](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeMergejoin.c#L1081-L1083)) |

#### 8.9 Lifecycle

| Event | State before | State after | Effect on later planning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ANALYZE` of a joined table | old most-common values and distinct counts | new ones | new join size estimates (chapter 4), hash bucket and skew estimates ([selfuncs.c#estimate_hash_bucket_stats-fraction](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/selfuncs.c#L3899-L3906)), Memoize `ndistinct` ([costsize.c#cost_memoize_rescan-hit-ratio](../../../../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L2549-L2599)) |
| New index on a join key | no parameterized inner index path | a parameterized path and presorted inputs | nested loops with index lookups (E7.13) and merge joins without sorts (E8.3) become possible |
| New foreign key between the joined tables | join size from column statistics | join size from the key (chapter 4, E4.7) | different estimates feed every method's cost |
| `SET join_collapse_limit` or `from_collapse_limit` | lists of up to 8 | longer or shorter lists | a wider or narrower search, as E8.8 shows |
| `SET geqo_threshold`, `geqo`, `geqo_effort`, `geqo_seed` | exhaustive below 12 items | a different switch point or genetic search | E8.9b against E8.9c |
| `SET work_mem` or `hash_mem_multiplier` | 4MB x 2 hash memory | more or less | batch counts, Memoize capacity, and hash-join eligibility for large MCVs (E8.10) |

All of these settings have `user` context: they apply to the session or transaction with `SET` (E16.1).
